A size that a call cannot fix refuses the call, also inside an overload set, instead of dropping the arm (row 400, its compiled half open). Every static argument but an operator counts in the exclusion rule; booleans join once the checker has boolean parameters (row 406). A size used as a value converts to `ZZ32` as a numeral does (row 485). The api's 25 unused sizes (F-35) go only by a diff shown to him with the switch-over's design.
40	- P-41 **At run time a size travels as the descriptor that a type argument has (design B).** It fills the slot that the team's code generator reserved. Each number has one descriptor, from a table, with no holder class, as the team instantiates types. Operator static arguments stay compile-time names (F-39): he sees no need to unify them.
41	- P-42 **An unbounded type parameter's implicit bound is `Any`, not `Object`.** `Any` holds tuples, functions and `()`, which `Object` does not, and the library instantiates its generic containers at tuples, arrays indexed by pairs among them. The specification states the bound, with a callout that keeps the Working Draft's `Object`. The compile path's `Object` bound departs from it until the switch-over (row 412).
42	- P-43 **The exclusion rule stays, and the number tower is flat (route A).** The compiled checker keeps the multiple instantiation exclusion rule. So the library's numbers are flat, as the team (Chase, Ryu, Maessen and Allen) flattened the compiler prelude in 2009 and 2010. The fixed widths, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`, each with its own algebra, and `Number` has no catch-all operators. Why: the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way, and its route leads to the POPL 2019 paper, which keeps the rule. He cares that specialised code runs fast, not how a specialisation is chosen. F-46 prices a return to route C.
43	- P-44 **`AnyIntegral`'s closure stands, and the checker reads `comprises` the 2012 way.** The closure `AnyIntegral comprises { ... }` stands, with a `NOT YET` comment in the team's wording. A generic child of a closed trait may extend it when every type that the checker knows below it is listed. The clause's text and walk stay as they are. Row 487 records the hole that every reading but the 2008 one shares: a program's own `Integral` subtype in another component is not caught.

A numeral whose candidate types are incomparable reads as `ZZ32`, or as `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by its magnitude. Why: generic code is never fast, and he wants code that a JVM can specialise. The rule is the team's later word (POPL 2019). He ranks the team's later work above his own reading. It sets the instance, not which declaration runs (P-46). MicroGPT's types are concrete, so it is untouched. The library keeps the team's unbounded declarations. 49	- P-50 **A `label` body takes the expected type of the whole `label` (item 48 (a)).** The specification types a `label` as the union of its body's last expression and its exits' `with` values. 50	- P-51 **A call written as another call's argument is retried against each declaration's parameter type (item 48 (b), row 455).** When the checker's attempts at a call keep none, an argument that is a call with inferred static arguments is checked again, with each candidate's parameter type as its expected type. 52	- P-53 **`String`'s `left` and `right` answer `Just(c)` (item 42, row 606).** For a non-empty string they return `Just` of the first and of the last character, as their declared `Maybe[\Char\]` and every other `left` and `right` of the library do. 54	- P-55 **A size may hold arithmetic, compared by its written form once numerals are folded (item 15, 15a with (b)).** The checker accepts a sum, difference, product or power in a size. `2 3` folds to `6`, but `s0 s1` is not `s1 s0`. The class loader computes the value when it makes a class. A size name may equal a numeral, as the team's Q&A answers, so the `N[\0\]` arm of a `typecase N[\b0\]` is reachable. The library keeps the team's sizes written as products and sums. Two later array forks stand at defaults while his answers are pending: fork 3, a size known only at run time, at way 4a, where his reading of P-40 is asked; and fork 2, the bound of `Vector` and `Matrix`, at the two-trait bound (PLAN items 13 and 52).
55	- P-56 **The open range `(:)` keeps its wildcard type, and its five cutting methods fail (item 49, row 656).** `TrivialOpenRange` stays `OpenRange[\Any\]`. A range over `ZZ32` is not a range over `Any`, so no body can type its `truncL`, `truncR`, `every`, `imposeStride` and `atMost`. They are `fail` bodies with a message, the team's own device for such a body. Nothing in the tree calls them on `(:)`. Way (c), `(:)` over `ZZ32`, is not taken: probe P3 found it changes 64 small programs' values.
56	- P-57 **`LexicographicReduction.isLeftZero` takes `TotalComparison`, so the team's answers are reached (row 582).** The team's overload `isLeftZero(_:Comparison)` is declared over `TotalComparison`, so the inherited `ReductionWithZeroes.isLeftZero` no longer shadows it. `LessThan` and `GreaterThan` answer `true`, and `EqualTo` `false`. `isLeftZero(Unordered)` is refused under walk. Nothing calls `isLeftZero`. Why: it cleared the count stage's last api error (F-53).
57	- P-58 **Every native binding is a `builtinPrimitive` call naming a static helper (item 35).** Each binding stays the library's own form, a body that is exactly `builtinPrimitive("…")`, and its string names a static helper of `nativeHelpers/`, not an interpreter glue class. Walk loads the string through a loader beside its glue classes. The compiled path rewrites each body at the parse into a synthetic `import java` and a call before the checker, and refuses a string that names no helper. Way 2, `import java` blocks in the library, is not taken. Still to build: the natives rungs, PLAN phase 4.

After the switch-over walk takes the static coercions that the checker inserts. MicroGPT's static types are concrete, so both paths agree on it.

Why: the proof addendum (`reviews/comprises-type-level-proof-addendum.md`) shows this sound for ground declarations, `G[\ZZ32\]` among them, with the coverage search local to overload checking. 62	### Numbers
63	
64	- P-66 **The integer principle: Java's and the JVM's defaults stay where they make sense, and are corrected where they fail high performance or mathematical precision.** The team did so with rounding and the sign of `GCD`. A hardware behaviour that bytecode can express gets its own explicit spelling, as the specification's wrapping and saturating operators do. Where the JVM prevents a correct implementation, the project gives way for now. The peers to compare are Julia, X10, Swift and Rust.
65	- P-67 **`round` on an exact half goes to the even integer, on both paths.** It is the specification's rule for rationals, IEEE's default and the team's own rational body. Built.
66	- P-68 **`floor` and `ceiling` on the float types keep the float; ⌊x⌋, ⌈x⌉, `round` and `truncate` return the unbounded ℤ.** The library's own `truncate` and `round` are tidied to match. Shifted-out bits fall silently, as in every peer language. Compiled code shifts the machine word, never through ℤ. A count may have any integral width (row 380). Built on both paths; the compiled path gets `shift` and the any-width count at the switch-over (P-38).
68	- P-70 **`GCD` and `LCM` give nonnegative results, and `LCM` raises an overflow error when the multiple does not fit, on both paths.** The specification says so. Built (row 334).
69	- P-71 **`|0|`, `-0` and `0 DIV -1` do not overflow: an overflow guard tests for the most negative value itself, not for `a = -a`.** The compiled natives and their siblings with that guard are fixed. Built (row 333).
70	- P-72 **`narrow` out of range truncates to the low 32 bits, signed and unsigned, on both paths.** The team's boundary test `tests/UnsignedTest.fss` asserts it. Built (row 346).
71	- P-73 **Fixed-width overflow raises `IntegerOverflow` under `walk`, as the specification says and the compiled path does, `NN32` and `NN64` included.** Code that means to wrap uses the specification's operators ∔, ∸ and ⨰, fully parenthesised, since their precedence is stated only among themselves. 72	- P-74 **Mixed integer widths convert by declared coercions (answer 8, to PLAN item 8): each wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one, as the compiler prelude does.** An exact conversion is implicit and a lossy one explicit: `ZZ32` and integer numerals coerce into `RR64`, and `ZZ64` into `RR64` stays explicit (P-66). A generic call or a range over mixed widths infers the narrowest type that both sides coerce into. The specification's `widens` is deferred. Built; no model line changed.
73	- P-75 **`NN32` coerces into `RR64`, since the conversion is exact (P-74).** Not built: with that coercion, a `ZZ32` with an `NN32` is ambiguous between `RR64`'s and `ZZ64`'s operators on both paths, where P-74 gives `ZZ64`, and two team tests fail (row 575). It waits as PLAN item 37, with its candidates; not building it is the default.

A range of rank 2 or 3 is a tuple of `ZZ32` ranges, and the public range traits stay generic in their index type. Built.
76	- P-78 **`SUM` and `PROD` without the `Number` catch-all: one generic reduction each over the library's algebra, taking its identity from the static argument (answer 7, to PLAN item 7).** A clause form whose element type nothing at the call fixes writes its static argument, as the team's tests do; `SUM e` and `DOT` keep their text. The model's two changed lines, `MicroGptFlat.fss:28` and `:43`, are approved. `BIG MAXN`, `BIG MINN` and `BIG MINMAXN` are gone, and `MAX` and `MIN` get no identity on the integers or the floats (F-60). Built.
77	- P-79 **The team's demos that write no static argument for a generic reduction stay as they are, and are respelled later only if they still fail.** When a batch has a free slot, it first checks each demo again under P-48's bound rule (row 425). 80	### Arrays and the model program
81	
82	- P-84 **Storage is `double[]`, unboxed, and arrays keep the team's `nat` sizes.** A high-performance language cannot box its array elements, and the sizes are central to the team's design. So both are built together: sized types, the checker taught `nat` parameters, in the library's own patterns. How `double[]` goes under a float vector is array decision A (P-85).
83	- P-85 **The array design's three questions are open, with no default, and return after the switch-over with array decisions A, B and D (PLAN item 13).** The three: a store per element type chosen by the factory, the size also kept as a field of the store, and a factory for a size known only at run time that returns the unsized `Array`. A is how `double[]` goes under a float vector, B where unboxed arithmetic happens, D sizes in the model's own types (P-87). Also open: why `RR64` and not `RR32`, since LLMs train at FP32 at most; the one reason given is the Python reference's float64 output. P-55 holds the forks taken before the switch-over.
84	- P-86 **The integration review's checks stand for the array work.** A generic `Vector` or `Matrix` body is checked against what each operation needs, with no blanket ring bound that would exclude integer arrays. An empty reduction is checked for its type and its value. A small product through `PView` and a transpose is checked, with controls. The checks: `reviews/numeric-hierarchy-integration-review.md` section 5.
85	- P-87 **The model's text is the notation, and the vocabulary is repaired around it.** An operator in the model never becomes a function call to satisfy an overload check. Any repair that changes a model line is shown to him as a diff before it is built. Decision D, the sized signatures of the flat program C4's vocabulary, is such a diff (`reviews/decision-d-diff.md`); nothing of it is applied before PLAN phase 5.
86	- P-88 **The model's vocabulary leaves `+`, `-` and `MAX` between an array and a scalar to the library's scalar block, and its diagonal keeps its own product.** `Diag` extends `Matrix` and overrides `mul`, as the type system promises (row 299). 87	- P-89 **`fill` takes a value, `tabulate` a function (answer 10).** It is his answer to PLAN item 10. `fill` keeps the value form, every peer language's meaning of the word, and the function form takes Scala's name `tabulate`. Built; no model line changed.
88	- P-90 **`Maybe`'s empty case is the team's parametric `Nothing[\T\]`, in the one library and the specification.** The bare `Nothing` is future work: it needs a `where` clause that binds a type variable in an `extends` clause, which neither path implements, and it is not tried before then. Gating row 331 on static-argument inference instead is parked (PLAN, "Off the path, parked").
89	- P-91 **What an object with no `asString` prints: its bare Fortress type name, walk's spelling, on both paths.** The debug marker he had in mind goes in `asDebugString`. Built, but for an object with a member named `toString`, which still overflows the stack when compiled (row 321).
90	
91	### The specification's revision
92	
93	- P-95 **Every change to the specification is recorded with its reason.** No discrepancy between the specification and the implementation stays open to confuse a reader. The original text and the reasons are kept, so that route C, the way back to the patents' forest rule (P-43), stays open. Every change takes the S1 form (P-96). `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is never touched.
94	- P-96 **The S1 form: a change of the specification is shown in the layered form that the team used for 1.0 and its 2009 draft.** A callout that prints in every build, not a `\note`, marks each changed passage. Appendix I's revival section gives each change its reason, its original text, the way back to route C and the decision it follows. The front matter has one paragraph on the revision, and a repository document holds the full reasoning. The unrevised copy is cited as the Working Draft of February 2011. The parts in detail: fortress-repo skill, `references/specification.md`.
95	- P-97 **The refused examples (S2) take the one library's shapes, under one statement of instantiation exclusion.** Each refused example stays, marked "Not allowed" as the specification marks one, beside the library's shape. The rule is stated once, in Luchangco's two-part form (P-25). The covariance example's callout adds that the type group's later design has a `covariant` modifier, which neither path implements (row 404). The calculi of Appendix A keep their rules, under a callout that they predate the rule.
96	- P-98 **`TotalComparison` extends `StandardMinMax[\TotalComparison\]`, so that it has `MIN` and `MAX`.** It does so in the api and in the component, and keeps its five restated members. He took it on the coordinator's recommendation and wants it explained in more detail when he has the energy, so it is on the list for his review (PLAN, "Pavol's answers, in the order they are needed").
97	
98	### The suites and the gate
99	
100	- P-102 **Test first, the test kept.** Every sealed-tree edit starts from a failing test added to the corpus: the worker writes the test first, verifies that it actually fails, makes the fix, proves it passes, and the test stays in the corpus from then on; the full suite stays green. The test needs no commit of its own: the test and the fix may land in one commit. How the test is written is in the `fortress-repo` skill's tests part.
101	- P-103 **The suite's verdict is the check.** A test passes or fails, as the team designed the suite, and a value that matters is asserted in the test with the mechanisms the suite already has (an `assert` in an interpreter test, `run_out_equals` in a compiled one). What a test prints beyond its checks does not matter. So no expected-output files are added; none of it is offered to him again.
102	- P-123 **Row 366's three-line fix waits for a rung of its own, and route C gets no entry in the specification's Proposed Features.** Both are batch 5's defaults, which he took: the fix is not in design B as he decided it (P-41), and Appendix I already carries route C, the alternative to the flat tower (P-96).
103	- P-124 **The specification's examples join the gate at zero red.** `ant testSpecData` runs them under walk as a gate step, and every example must pass. A failing example is not respelled for walk, and no list of known red examples is kept: the implementation is fixed instead. Built.
104	- P-125 **The suites run Fortress in parallel, pinned at four threads in `build.xml`.** Parallelism is native to Fortress, so a one-thread suite has a blind spot, and sparing a four-CPU machine is no reason for one. A test that fails or varies under parallelism is written wrong, such as a write that needs `atomic`, or it exposes a defect: either is fixed, never hidden by a pin. The pin makes every run the same, whatever the calling shell sets. Built.

<!-- The curator's decisions about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as they stand now. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- P-48 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `POSITIONS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. How the curator and the coordinator work is that skill's, and what is established is in `FACTS.md`; neither is repeated here. -->

# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground

## The goal

- P-7 **The goal is to finish what the designers intended, measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to bytecode and running fast.** The judge is `Specification/`, the Working Draft of February 2011 as the revival revises it, with the 2012 Types chapter cited beside it (P-25). The language is not redesigned. The specification is a living document that states the revival's changes (P-95). The floor to measure against is a pure-Java microGPT, not yet written (PLAN phase 6).
- P-8 **Where the designers left no word, he decides by the goal, a compiled microGPT running fast, not by type-theoretic purity, and stays true to the spirit of Fortress.** He accepts the language's unfinished corners rather than stall in theory. He has not read the specification, the type papers or the library, and takes the designers to have known more than he does. So a review checks his decisions against their intent, for errors of commission and of omission; its items are decisions in this file. Detail: `reviews/decisions-review/judgement.md`, "In short".
- P-9 **The search is for microGPT's most readable expression.** In his words, "we are searching for the optimal expression of the microGPT algorithm for readability." The specification's `T^n` denotes these traits (row 24), and neither path takes it. Detail: `reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 2.
- F-154 **The library declares its products with shared `nat`s, so under walk a product of the wrong shapes stops the run at dispatch.** The products are `Matrix[\T,n,m\]` by `Matrix[\T,m,p\]`, and the matrix-vector and vector-matrix pairs. The stop is a `ProgramError` that no `catch` takes (row 254). For an overloaded name it reads "Failed to find any matching overload". For a name that is not overloaded it is a unification error that names the size. Detail: `apl/mg/NOTES-swap.md`, "What the shared nats catch: the mismatch probe".
- F-155 **Under walk, two declarations of one name that differ only in the element type, or a rank-specialised declaration beside an index-generic one, are refused at load.** The message is "at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types" (rows 159, 416). Walk checks as one family the overloads of one name that two imported apis declare, and an import alias does not separate them. So two such vocabularies cannot stand in one component. Detail: `apl/mg/NOTES-swap.md`, "Departures, each with its evidence", items 5 and 6.
- F-156 **The library has no reshape, plane, gather, outer product or ravel, and the comment on its scalar-extension block is the revival's, not the team's.** That comment (F-119) says that a static checker loses a sized argument's rank and size in the block's result. The team's own statement on per-type storage is Maessen's commit message on the unboxed `RR64` array, `353818213`; a claim of the team's intent cites it. Detail: `run-c4/probes/vocabulary/REPORT.md`, section A; `reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 9.
- F-157 **An array is a trait with `get` and `put`, and a view is an object that implements it over other storage, the language's own idiom.** Under walk the library's row slice `m[i,:]` costs five times a six-line user view (row 298). A diagonal as a `Matrix` view costs 13 to 54 times a row-scaling operator (row 299). A subtype of `Matrix` that overrides `mul` gets its own product through the library's operators, which forward to `mul`. It needs no api line, since walk dispatches the method on the receiver's run-time type. Detail: `run-c4/probes/vocabulary/diag-override.md`, "Result".
- F-158 **`fill` takes a value and `tabulate` a function, both defined where the array diamond meets.** It builds P-89. `StandardMutableArrayType` and `ImmutableArray1`, the traits below both sides of the diamond, define them. A method declared only in each leaf leaves the meet refused by the checker's Meet Rule, so `copy` is declared on the meet too (row 467). Its factories are `tabulatedArray1` to `tabulatedArray3` and `tabulatedVector`. A demo still passes a function to `fill` (row 464). Gated by `tests/TabulateRungA.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-tabulate/REPORT.md` section 2.
- F-159 **A store written for `RR64` alone is selected under the generic array traits by the library's witness `typecase` and its `cast`, on both paths.** A witness `typecase` whose `RR64` arm returns that store runs under walk, and the checker refuses its union type. Wrapped in the library's `cast`, as `additiveIdentity` does, it checks, and both paths pick the `RR64` store only for `RR64`. A plain factory beside the generic one also works compiled; walk's load check (F-27) has not been run on that pair. It bears on array decision A (P-85). Detail: `reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 3.
## The specification and the repository's lineage

- F-162 **Citing `Specification/library/apis/*.tex` as an independent standard is circular.** The team says that the library part "is largely automatically generated from the API code" (`Specification/library/structure.tex:25-31`). The build renders the listings from the `.fsi` files, and they are not in the tree. So a listing cannot justify an edit of the `.fsi` file, and an api edit changes the PDF there. Cite the `.fsi` line. The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/specification.md` holds the rule.
- F-163 **The in-repo `Specification/` is the one prose to search; `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is byte for byte the Working Draft of 2011-02-02, and only its `fortress.1.0.pdf` is the 1.0 text.** `git diff --quiet 2f8b4331a:Specification c02fa44d0:Specification-1.0-frozen` succeeds. The team left Appendix I, the changes appendix, a stub. `Specification/fortress.pdf` is a draft build, so the team's `\note` boxes print. The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/specification.md` says how to cite and change each copy. Detail: `reviews/spec-change-form.md` sections 5 and 7.
- F-165 **The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, and `main` descends from `8fe1daa8f`, which copied a third-party Java 9 port onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`.** The port shares no history with this tree, and most of its 1,506 files are removed or redone. One running piece stays, the `FTypeArrayList` fix for the JDK 8 `TreeSet` crash; `lineage.md` lists the rest for removal. The branch `clean-ladder` (`8332bd34f`) rebuilds on `a874948ac` without the port and never replaced `main`. Detail: `coordinator/lineage.md`, "The facts".
- F-166 **The team's latest word on types and on the exclusion rule is the unfinished restart, not `Specification/`.** The restart, `Documentation/Specification/`, was never adopted. Its Types chapter restates the exclusion rule as "instantiation exclusion" and adds `covariant`. On static parameters, traits, exceptions, components and the numeric library, `Specification/` is the only statement. Later than both, the type group's POPL 2019 paper gives P-48's instance rule. Its calculus bars a method type parameter from an upper bound, so its soundness proof does not cover the library's F-bounded functions, such as `SUM` and `BIG MAX`. `reviews/decisions-review/popl-recheck.md` checks the curator's decisions against it. Detail: `coordinator/spec-lineage.md` section 6; `research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md` sections 6 and 8.
- F-167 **The specification states instantiation exclusion, and its refused examples are the library's shapes; the calculi of Appendix A carry a callout that they predate the rule.** It builds P-97. It also bars a `where`-clause variable from an `extends` clause's static arguments. Each refused example stays, marked "Not allowed", beside the library's shape, which runs on both paths except `Nothing[\String\]` on the compiled prelude (row 331). The checker does not yet refuse two cases (rows 406, 414). Detail and examples: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md` sections 2 and 3.
- F-168 **The specification's number chapters describe the flat library, and its advanced chapter on rational quantities stays word for word as a superseded design.** The eight number types are siblings under `Number` (F-131). They convert by the library's coercions, and every other conversion is explicit, such as `asFloat(x)`. Refined types are gone. ℚ holds +∞, −∞ and 0/0, and claims neither a field nor a total order. The integer `^` has no result for a negative power. The chapters state P-74 and P-78. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-numbers/decision-record.md` section 3.
- F-169 **The Working Draft never wrote static-argument inference, a numeral's type or a range's integer width; the specification's text on all three is the revival's.** The Working Draft's inference chapter is a heading and notes, and its ranges section names no integer type. The later restart adds nothing on the three. So a citation of the specification on them cites the revival, not the team. The revised text states F-173's inference rule and F-170's ranges, and gives an integer numeral the type `IntLiteral` (P-76). Detail: `reviews/numerics-plan-coordinator/evidence-B.md` sections 1 and 2.
- F-170 **The specification's ranges are over ℤ32, and its own ranges over wider integer types are respelled.** An integer numeral and a `nat` or `int` parameter convert into a range's ℤ32 components. Another integer type is a static error. A wider counter widens each element (row 485). The two examples that built `ZZ64` ranges run over ℤ32, and `ant testSpecData`, a gate step, runs both (F-114). Under walk a `nat` parameter in value position is an `Int`, refused at an `NN32` binding (row 486). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-ranges/decision-record.md` sections 2 and 3.
- F-171 **The specification reads a `comprises` clause as the later Types chapter does: every value of the trait is a value of a listed type, and a trait with static parameters may stand unlisted between.** A listed type may be an instantiation at the trait's static parameters or `where`-clause variables. A listed bare type variable stays open (row 407). The checker departs in rows 487, 489 and 490. Whether the team's commented `comprises Integral[\I\] where [\I\]` is valid is open (F-121). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-comprises/decision-record.md` section 2.
- F-172 **The specification states the library's integer rules, the coercion example with the exclusions its definition needs, and the rational type's library algebra.** It states `narrow`, `LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT` on the five integer types, `shift` exact at any count, and nonnegative `GCD` and `LCM`. A fixed-size result that the type cannot hold throws `IntegerOverflow`. The coercion example runs on both paths (row 394). `QQ` extends the library's four algebraic traits, their laws holding for the finite rationals. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-integer-rules/decision-record.md` section 2.
- F-173 **The specification's type-inference chapter states the rule the compiled checker builds.** It states P-46, P-48 and P-49: the declaration is chosen first, then its static arguments are inferred. A lone type parameter takes the narrowest of its arguments' types and their coercion targets, else its bound; one that nothing fixes takes its bound, never `BottomType`. The checker departs only at `ZZ32` with `NN32` on the compiler prelude (row 442). Callouts give walk's departures (rows 587, 589, 591, 592, 616). Plain tests gate the lone parameter on both paths: `compiler_tests/InferLone*` and `tests/InferLone*Walk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-inference/decision-record.md` section 3.1.
- F-174 **The specification states the type group's 2011 overloading model: declarations of one name may differ in their static parameters, and a declaration with static parameters is read over its instances.** It states P-45 and P-42. A new section states the OOPSLA 2011 paper's three rules, with the positional rule as the compiled path's restriction. The naked-`Any` rule is against a written `Any` (row 534). Each path fails some sets that the rules accept, and Appendix I names them (rows 159, 537, 539, 542). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md` sections 3 and 4.
- F-175 **The specification gives the run-time instance of a dispatched declaration by the POPL 2019 paper's rule, and reads a `comprises` clause at the level of values in every passage.** It builds P-48 and P-60. The dispatch paragraph's callout says that both paths take the value's type where the value does not fix the parameter (row 538, gated by `compiler_tests/XXXGenericInstanceUnfixed`), and that the compiled path does not yet run its second example (row 496). F-173 gives the inference chapter. Appendix I names rows 487, 540, 543, 546 and 547. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md` sections 5 to 9.
- F-176 **The specification allows arithmetic in a size, and two size expressions are the same type when they are written alike once numerals are folded.** It states P-55. A size may be a numeral, a name, a sum, a difference, a product, a power to a numeral or a name, or a bracketed expression. A static parameter is not known to differ from a numeral. F-146 gives the compiled checker. Walk computes `+`, `-` and juxtaposition at instantiation, stops on a power (row 676), and binds only a name or a numeral at a call. Source: `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:49-62`.
## The territory map

- F-179 **Tasks and transactions are implemented twice, in `interpreter/evaluator/` and in `runtimeSystem/`, independently.** A fix in one copy does not reach the other: row 302's fix is in the compiled copy only. Detail: `coordinator/map/modules-and-phases.md`, "B.11 The runtime".
- F-180 **`import java` is wired on walk through `ForeignComponentWrapper` and `ClosureMaker`, but five gaps stop it and no test uses it.** Six small patches close them in a probe. P-58 binds the natives by `builtinPrimitive` instead; both halves of that way ran as probes. Two findings bear on any binding text that both paths share. A helper that raises a Fortress exception names a compiled-prelude class, which walk ends as a `FortressImplementationError`. A helper over compiled-world types cannot take walk's values. Detail: `perf-probes/prelude/natives-shape.md` section 1.
- F-181 **The code generator refuses every function, object and trait declaration that carries a `where` clause or a contract (row 701).** The `fortress-repo` skill's `references/compiler.md`, "What the compiled path cannot compile yet", gives this refusal and the constructs that the code generator has no case for, a local function among them (row 304). An array comprehension has no case either. Detail: `coordinator/map/spec-to-implementation.md` section 3.
- F-182 **Both paths refuse `type` aliases, `test` and `property` declarations, in the index builder that the repository runs (`scala_src/typechecker/IndexBuilder.scala:187-189`).** Neither path implements them. Detail: `coordinator/map/spec-to-implementation.md` section 3.
- F-183 **The compiled path's only array-like types are `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`, two hand-written Java classes declared only in its prelude and absent from the specification.** Each element access is boxed, and no gated test makes or indexes one at run time. Passed to a generic object's constructor, one fails at load: its descriptor class is `RTTIv`, where stamped code asks for `RTTIc` (row 408, `compiler_tests/XXXVecCtorLoad`). A native helper cannot take a Java array, since the wrapper generator skips such methods. Detail: `compiler-probes/vectors/vectors.md` sections 1 and 7.
- F-184 **A generic object referenced without its static arguments is a static error on the compiled path, and the checker never consults the expected type for it.** `b: Box[\ZZ32\] = Box` fails as an ill-formed type, and a bare `Empty` as an argument or a field's default as an internal error, `T is not in the kind env`. Walk fails on both. Writing the static argument avoids both. So a bare `Nothing` compiles only against the compiled prelude's own `Nothing` (row 331, P-90). Detail: `compiler-probes/maybe-inference/inference.md`.
- F-185 **The suites run two corpora ported by hand, and no test compares the two paths on one program.** `tests/` shares no file name with `compiler_tests/`, and its 11 names shared with `other_compiler_tests/` are other programs. `fortress.unittests.noopt=true` in `default_repository/configuration` turns off the bytecode optimizer's tests. `TransactionJUTest`'s multi-threaded half is commented out. By the map's one count, 121 `.fss` files in the suites' directories run in no test, and some directories are orphaned. Detail: `coordinator/map/test-coverage.md` sections A.1, A.4 and C.1.

# Boot note

Rewritten at 19:28 UTC on 2026-10-13, during the overnight run he approved at 17:13 UTC. The coordinating session runs on Opus 5.5 (his `/model` just before 21:19 UTC on 2026-10-12), as the tier rule has it (POSITIONS, "Which tier runs what"); every worker launch names its tier. The VM restarted at 17:13:11 UTC (`uptime -s`), the tree equal to origin and the scratchpad intact, so the cap's next stop is about 06:11 UTC on 2026-10-14 (08:11 his time). The platform's git-check Stop hook is back since the restarts (the original is in the session scratchpad as `stop-hook-git-check.sh.orig`); its reminders get ".". The overnight check-ins ran from 18:00 UTC to 21:46 UTC; the rest were deleted once the order was done.

**His approval of 17:13 UTC, for tonight without his reading in between:** "you have my approval to run overnight to the consolidated record, to this coordinator skill extraction, as well as the container skill using the processes we've established"; and two Fable adversarial reviews, of the record store design and of the skill outline. He went to a movie. His comments: the principles (nine, 15:25 to 16:03), the design (eight, 16:46 to 17:08: rebuild the history too, from primary sources, a full garbage collection now and incremental passes later), all on HELD.

**Running, as of 20:44 UTC:** nothing. Tonight's order is done. The morning page "Overnight Run, 13 October" is https://claude.ai/artifact/Sy6JBLaZqhLTJnUyYXBQoA (version 1, published 20:44 UTC, push notification sent; not watched, since the session holds its ten watches). It holds the sizes, the tests, the decisions for his review and the cost; his answers to it come one at a time. No check-in is armed: check-ins 7 to 10 were deleted at 21:46 UTC, since nothing runs. Since the last note: the chart on "Fortress Revival So Far", version 21 (`010775aaf`; only the figure and its caption's dates changed); scenario 6 on the final record, 3 of 3 (`4d478cc6a`); `check-verbatim.py` retired (`e78ed16b0`); PLAN's last citation by an old title (`8ded51772`). **Landed tonight:** the outline and its review (`d84be672f`, `65ef2e72b`); the design and its review (`92827fca8`, `cc9424c2a`); the entry definition (`8cde9406c`); `record.py` and the numbering (`a74f5a2b7`, `a88e52bf7`); nine chunks (`55f1a1352` to `ab933086b`): 361K to 200.6K; the record test, pilot 29 and final 30 of 30 against the old record's 28 (`c89529746`, `3ab48e178`); the writer's task (`912228df2`); the new `coordinator` skill (`7b434aae5`, fixed `f6bc1aa75`); the compaction hook (`86ec86f7c`); `fortress-repo`'s pieces and `cloud-container` rewritten (`4c11b10c3`, `30a6acaef`), their cold read (70 flags) fixed with P-135, F-210 and F-219's rules moved in (`8ca0d7e61`); step 12 (`1632b5dfa` to `88d9b1437`) and the last three removals (`b67abe3d2`): FACTS 257.8K to 90.2K and POSITIONS 102.9K to 33.9K, 360.6K to 124.1K; the boot reads 615.9K to 361.9K, INDEX now 55 % of them; the skills without `sources.md` 206.5K to 214.4K; README to the boot order, `protocol.md` retired; HELD's held and settled points closed (`0528e963b`). Cost since 14:40 UTC, at 20:10: about 10.9M written (workers 9.3M, the headless writers 0.6M, this session 1.0M). **Next:** the curator's reading of the morning page. **For the morning page, besides the chunk writers' points below:** the writers' decisions not taken (the review list's home in PLAN; the commit stage quoting the record part, which the batch script does not do today; the weekly limit in `stops.md`; the port named in `records.md`; `cloud-container`'s description gaining three triggers after its 20/20 score; the backup hook registered twice in this container); the task's reason wrong on the masks (the gate's tools mask only the time; `compare-normalised.py` masks the three); M3, the hook's reset in a changed form (the curator does it in manual mode); four history notes naming `cloud-container`'s old headings. **Owed after the consolidation, from the builder's report:** `check-verbatim.py` retired; the four live citations left by title (PLAN 2, `key.md` 2); `tools/test_ledger.py`, 10 of 13 tests failing already at HEAD's own code (stale expectations), a finding for the morning list.

- `explorations/coordinator/README.md`: The coordinating session's boot order, at session start and after every compaction, as the `coordinator` skill's boot section gives it; how the session works, and how the record is kept, is that skill (`.claude/skills/coordinator/`).

# The transcript backup and the git-check hook

This part is for the coordinating session. Two Stop hooks run in this container.

## The transcript backup

The backup's Stop hook runs `/home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded/scripts/backup.sh`. The hook returns at once, and a detached runner does the work. It copies the transcripts of every session in the container, Workflow agents' included, into that worktree of the orphan branch `transcripts-blinded`. Then it commits, pushes and packs. A pass takes about 10 s and writes one line to the worktree's `.backup.log`, which keeps the last 200.

The tracked `.claude/settings.json` registers the hook, beside the compaction hook. `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` adds it to `~/.claude/settings.json` only if the tracked file does not. If both files register it, each turn's end runs two passes, about 4 s apart, which the backup's lock runs one after the other. They do no harm.

Its blind spots:

- It runs when a turn of the main session ends, not when an agent finishes. A session inside one long turn is not backed up, however much its agents do. Check-ins end turns (`stops.md`).
- It copies transcripts, not trees. Uncommitted work in a worktree is not covered.
- If the container dies within about 10 s of a turn's end, that turn's snapshot is lost.
- It swallows every error and never holds up the session, so a failed push is silent. At each check-in and after each process stop, read the log's last line, or the branch's state. A good pass reads `push=ok`, or `ahead=0 push=none`.

      tail -1 /home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded/.backup.log
      git -C /home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded status -sb

- The runner removes only an `index.lock` that is at least 10 s old and that no process holds open. A stale `/home/user/fortress/.git/refs/heads/transcripts-blinded.lock` fails every later commit (`commit=failed` in the log). If no process holds it open, remove it by hand.

The scripts that run are the copies in the worktree's `scripts/`. The reference copies in `explorations/coordinator/transcript-backup/` change nothing until you copy them into the worktree. If a pass fails in a way that this section does not name, print `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/remote-container.md#Three traps'`, and the same for "How the snapshot works".

## The platform's git-check hook

`~/.claude/stop-hook-git-check.sh` comes from the launcher (`--settings /root/.claude/launcher-settings.json`). It exits 2, which makes the session take another turn, when the tree has uncommitted changes, untracked files, or unpushed commits. When commit signing is on, it also exits 2 for a local commit that is unsigned or whose committer is not `noreply@anthropic.com`.

Its reminders are advisory. While the tree holds work that is not ready to commit or push, decline a reminder: say in one line that the work is not ready, and end the turn. The hook does not fire again at the end of the turn that it started.

To turn the hook off, give the script an empty body, which reads its input and exits 0. Keep the original in the session's scratchpad:

    cp ~/.claude/stop-hook-git-check.sh <scratchpad>/stop-hook-git-check.sh.orig
    printf '#!/bin/bash\ncat >/dev/null\nexit 0\n' > ~/.claude/stop-hook-git-check.sh

- The automatic permission check refuses this step in auto mode, and also a check-in whose prompt would take it. The step runs only after the curator switches the session to manual approval, where each tool call waits for the curator.
- In manual approval, every command of a Workflow agent also waits for the curator's approval. So a batch runs unattended only in auto mode: after the step, ask the curator to switch back.
- Every start of the process writes the original script again. So after each process stop the hook is back on: `grep -c stop_hook_active ~/.claude/stop-hook-git-check.sh` prints 1 or more. The `coordinator` skill's `SKILL.md`, "The boot", says how the curator is told.

# Running and reviewing a batch

The batch workflow is `explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` and its manual, `climb-batch-workflow.md` beside it. Its stages run in this order: the scatter of the rungs, the rung workers, the skeptics, the judges and the repair round, the gather, the merged-diff review, the gate, and the commit stage. Read a stage's section of the manual when you reach it: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md#<heading>'`.

**batch record**
: `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-<name>.md`, written by the planner before the launch. Its rung sections are the workers' briefs; its other sections are for the curator.

**base**
: Commit that the batch starts from.

**gather**
: Stage that merges the rungs and folds their reports and record lines into the tree.

**merged-diff review**
: Review of the gathered diff, beside the gate, of the records, the reserved points and the routing.

**repair round**
: One round of fixes after the merged-diff review or the gate.

**commit stage**
: Last stage, which commits the landed tree and runs the pass of `references/record.md`.

**reserved point**
: Point that a batch record keeps for the curator, such as a model or APL line beyond the approved ones, or an interpreter output that a rung cannot explain.

**checker count**
: Errors that the compiled checker reports on the interpreter's library, up to each component's first error.

**distance**
: All the checker's errors on that library, which must reach zero before the switch-over: the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library.

## The go

- The batches of PLAN's phase 3 run on a standing go, in PLAN's order. Launch each when the batch before it has landed and its own batch record has no open question.
- Put a question that a batch record raises to the curator first. While the curator is away, overnight, take its recommended default and put it on the review list. If that default would reverse a decision of the curator, hold that batch, and launch the repair batch (`explorations/coordinator/REPAIR-BATCH.md`) in its place.
- A top-tier review of a coming batch's record, written for the curator in place of reading the record, needs no further ask.

## The workflow

- Between batches, improve the script and the manual where a batch showed a problem.
- Let every step spend the fewest workers that it needs.
- Build the base once, yourself, in a worktree where nobody compiles or runs (`args.baseBuild`). Every rung worktree is seeded from it (`explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh`), never built clean.
- No stage runs a build, a suite or a measurement again on a code state that another stage ran, and no agent reads again a log that has not changed.
- Let the planner give each rung its mission briefing, from the territory map (`explorations/coordinator/map/`), in neutral words: "the decisions on record", not the curator's name. Require no answers from the worker about how it searched.
- At each landing, report the share of agents that read the briefing in their first turn. Aim for about 80 percent, the share it once had; it fell to 25 to 35.

## The roles

- The skeptic checks a rung's result after its worker, and builds nothing to check. It reads from the worker's transcript whether the test came first and failed. It runs its own small programs on the rung's build, and on the base through `explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh` with a private caches folder.
- It checks the result against the library's way, the ledger, sibling sites and the decisions on record, and fixes what it finds, test first.
- A judge rules only on a fix that the skeptic marks contested, on a rung that the skeptic refuses, or on a rung whose worker reported that it could not go on. The first ruling runs on Opus, a second on Fable (`judgeTier`). A settled fix lands with the review and the gate as its check.
- No batch compares the printed outputs of the suites' test programs, and no baseline is run to compare against.

## The checker count and the distance

The gate reports the checker count in every batch, and the distance in phase 3. Neither turns the gate red.

- If a rung's test is the checker count or the distance, it takes the last landed gate's tables as its starting values.
- If every file that a rung changes lies outside what the two measures read, the rung runs neither and lists those files (`STAGE_BLIND`). Its skeptic checks the list against the branch's diff.
- The review after the batch ties every new or risen row of the count's table to a named rung edit.
- The gate's comparisons hide Java line numbers, identity hashes and moved library positions. Put every difference that they hid on the review list. Put there too each line of the team's tests that a rung rewrote to keep its checked value, with its before and after.

## Reserved points and repairs

- A reversible reserved point does not hold the batch. The batch lands with the point's default, and the point goes on the review list.
- An output that the base already varies from run to run, with the test's verdict unchanged, is a ledger row.
- After its one repair round, a merged-diff review that still blocks does not hold a batch whose gate is green. Its findings go on the review list, for the batch after. The review runs once in each batch.
- A repair after the gate runs the gate again only if it changes what the gate reads (its part in `fortress-repo`).
- If the gate over a merged batch is red, do not bisect. Find the cause as a whole, and rework that part in the merged batch. If the gate is still red after its repair, the batch does not land: put it to the curator at once, as a hold.

## While it runs

- At a boot, read the batch record's sections for the curator, the run's journal (`references/delegating.md`) at the run ID in the boot note, and the times of its agents' transcripts in the session's `subagents/workflows/<run>/`.
- Workers push to their own `wip/` branches as they go. A branch holds only what `main` is to hold (`fortress-repo`, its committing part).
- If a process stop or the usage limit ends the run, resume it (`references/delegating.md`). The limit drops no rung.

## The landing

1. Check that the commit stage folded the batch's entries into FACTS (`references/record.md`, "The pass").
2. Have the writer update `fortress-repo`'s `references/revival-changes.md` (`references/skill-rewrite.md`).
3. Name each decision that landed in one line, and put the items for the curator on the review list.
4. Have one Opus reviewer, which only reads, check the landed changes against the decisions on record and the library's way; measure misses by kind, the briefing's use and cost, and re-measuring; and run the routing check (the manual, "After the landing: the coordinator's routing").
5. File what the review finds in PLAN.

If that default would reverse a decision of the curator, hold that batch, and launch the repair batch (`explorations/coordinator/REPAIR-BATCH.md`) in its place.
- A top-tier review of a coming batch's record, written for the curator in place of reading the record, needs no further ask.

## The workflow

- Between batches, improve the script and the manual where a batch showed a problem.
- Let every step spend the fewest workers that it needs.
- Build the base once, yourself, in a worktree where nobody compiles or runs (`args.baseBuild`). Every rung worktree is seeded from it (`explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh`), never built clean.
- No stage runs a build, a suite or a measurement again on a code state that another stage ran, and no agent reads again a log that has not changed.
- Let the planner give each rung its mission briefing, from the territory map (`explorations/coordinator/map/`), in neutral words: "the decisions on record", not the curator's name. Require no answers from the worker about how it searched.
- At each landing, report the share of agents that read the briefing in their first turn. Aim for about 80 percent, the share it once had; it fell to 25 to 35.

## The roles

- The skeptic checks a rung's result after its worker, and builds nothing to check. It reads from the worker's transcript whether the test came first and failed. It runs its own small programs on the rung's build, and on the base through `explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh` with a private caches folder.
- It checks the result against the library's way, the ledger, sibling sites and the decisions on record, and fixes what it finds, test first.
- A judge rules only on a fix that the skeptic marks contested, on a rung that the skeptic refuses, or on a rung whose worker reported that it could not go on. The first ruling runs on Opus, a second on Fable (`judgeTier`). A settled fix lands with the review and the gate as its check.
- No batch compares the printed outputs of the suites' test programs, and no baseline is run to compare against.

## The checker count and the distance

The gate reports the checker count in every batch, and the distance in phase 3. Neither turns the gate red.

- If a rung's test is the checker count or the distance, it takes the last landed gate's tables as its starting values.
- If every file that a rung changes lies outside what the two measures read, the rung runs neither and lists those files (`STAGE_BLIND`). Its skeptic checks the list against the branch's diff.
- The review after the batch ties every new or risen row of the count's table to a named rung edit.
- The gate's comparisons hide Java line numbers, identity hashes and moved library positions. Put every difference that they hid on the review list. Put there too each line of the team's tests that a rung rewrote to keep its checked value, with its before and after.

## Reserved points and repairs

- A reversible reserved point does not hold the batch. The batch lands with the point's default, and the point goes on the review list.
- An output that the base already varies from run to run, with the test's verdict unchanged, is a ledger row.
- After its one repair round, a merged-diff review that still blocks does not hold a batch whose gate is green. Its findings go on the review list, for the batch after. The review runs once in each batch.
- A repair after the gate runs the gate again only if it changes what the gate reads (its part in `fortress-repo`).
- If the gate over a merged batch is red, do not bisect. Find the cause as a whole, and rework that part in the merged batch. If the gate is still red after its repair, the batch does not land: put it to the curator at once, as a hold.

## While it runs

- At a boot, read the batch record's sections for the curator, the run's journal (`references/delegating.md`) at the run ID in the boot note, and the times of its agents' transcripts in the session's `subagents/workflows/<run>/`.
- Workers push to their own `wip/` branches as they go. A branch holds only what `main` is to hold (`fortress-repo`, its committing part).
- If a process stop or the usage limit ends the run, resume it (`references/delegating.md`). The limit drops no rung.

## The landing

1. Check that the commit stage folded the batch's entries into FACTS (`references/record.md`, "The pass").
2. Have the writer update `fortress-repo`'s `references/revival-changes.md` (`references/skill-rewrite.md`).
3. Name each decision that landed in one line, and put the items for the curator on the review list.
4. Have one Opus reviewer, which only reads, check the landed changes against the decisions on record and the library's way; measure misses by kind, the briefing's use and cost, and re-measuring; and run the routing check (the manual, "After the landing: the coordinator's routing").
5. File what the review finds in PLAN.

# Delegating: briefing, launching, watching and resuming workers

**Workflow run**
: Run of a script by the Workflow tool, which launches one agent for each `agent()` call.

**journal**
: Workflow run's log, `journal.jsonl` in `~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>/subagents/workflows/<run>/`: one `launched` line, then a `started` line for each agent call and a `result` line with its structured result.

**headless session**
: `claude -p` session started from your shell.

**archaeology**
: Search of git and the transcripts for how something came about. It returns cited evidence, not a judgement.

## Which tier runs what

- Give each worker its tier's alias: `model: 'opus'`, `'sonnet'` or `'fable'`. Write no identifier that an alias resolves to.
- Use Sonnet for archaeology and retrieval only, never for a judgement.
- When this session runs on Fable, have an Opus worker write each longer report or page for the curator.
- Take a cross-area question in two steps. First, Opus workers gather cited evidence or a list of ways. Then, if the record does not settle it, run a Fable judgement without asking, sparingly, and put it to the curator as an ask.
- Three kinds of Fable work have a go in advance: a judge's second ruling in a batch, the top-tier reviews of the batch records, and the comparison of a rewritten skill part with the version that the curator approved. Ask first for any other Fable worker, such as one on your own conduct, one whose answer would reverse the curator's decision, or a Fable and an Opus worker run apart on one question.
- Weigh a Fable review's ideas critically: it tends to keep everything as it was. An Opus worker is enough for a check.
- A Fable token also uses the all-models limits, at three to four times an Opus token's share of the session limit.

## What a brief holds

- The problem, never the expected answer. On a design choice, ask the worker to list every way that the language and the library offer, and give it none of our notes or options.
- If a rule blocks an option, ask how the library gets around it.
- A pointer to the research on file, not a restatement of it.
- The record's measurements, as findings to cite, not claims to check again, even for a worker kept clean of our options. Name the one new thing to measure. Ask for a new measurement only if the tree has changed under a finding, and say what changed.
- The entries that it needs, quoted word for word under their numbers. Quote a rule of the curator's whole, with its limit and its example.
- For an update of a document: a length cap against the version before. The update adds what landed.
- No second reader named in the brief, since that reframes the document.
- No request to measure or cap its own token spend. The spend is yours to watch.
- For an Agent-tool worker: every wait under 270 s. A long run is polled in steps, or handed to a script while the agent ends its turn.

A worker whose task touches the repository loads `fortress-repo` by itself. That skill tells it which choices are its own.

## Watching a run

- If you launch a long or large run outside a batch, such as a probe that builds and runs suites for an hour, write its estimate of tokens written in the boot note. A probe can write ten times its estimate.
- Watch its spend: `spend.py <since-epoch> <path>`, where the path is the session's `subagents/` folder for agents, or the project's folder for headless sessions. If it passes the estimate, give the worker an instruction or end it. Watch no other run this way.
- When an overnight or long run starts, arm its check-ins: `send_later` reminders 45 minutes apart, in one turn (`cloud-container`, its stops part). An hourly check-in would let the cache expire.
- Keep each wait of yours under an hour. The `Monitor` tool can watch a run.
- If a worker waits on the curator between tasks, run it as a headless session and resume it within the hour (`--resume <id>`).

## Interrupts and process stops

An interrupt or a process stop kills every running Workflow agent and Agent-tool worker (`fortress-repo`, its session part). A compaction between turns leaves a Workflow run alive.

- After an accidental interrupt, tell the curator, and resume the run.
- Resume a Workflow run, never relaunch it: `resumeFromRunId`, with the same script and arguments as at launch, byte for byte. A finished agent keeps its result. An unfinished one runs from its start, on its worktree's leftovers.
- The resume reuses the longest unchanged prefix of `agent()` calls, in call order. A hash given short where the launch gave it in full misses from the first call.
- If the script has changed since launch, resume from a copy as launched: `git show <launch commit>:<path>`. If the call order would differ, wrap `agent()` in the copy, so that the finished calls come in the journal's order of `started` lines. `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/design-batch10-opus.md` has such a wrapper (`resumeOrder`).
- If a batch's commit stage was killed before it committed, its edits are in `/home/user/fortress`. Resume with a commit prompt that names them.
- If a batch's gather was killed mid-work, `git stash` its staged changes and keep the stash before you resume.
- A new session cannot resume another session's run.
- An Agent-tool worker that a process stop killed goes on from its transcript on a `SendMessage`. One that an interrupt killed cannot. Relaunch it only at the curator's explicit ask, and tell the new worker its predecessor's leftovers.
- Give a Fable successor the leftovers in the tree, never the transcript: the safety filter can end a Fable worker that prints one.

## The Workflow tool

- The tool runs at most two agents at once on this machine. The others wait.
- Across agents, the cache serves the first message only when the whole prompt is identical. A project agent type's system prompt is cached for every agent of the type, so put text that every agent needs there.
- A project agent type written during the session is found only after a process stop. A project skill appears at once.
- `agent()` can return null for an agent that the harness marks failed after it delivered its result. Read its branch before you run it again.
- Check a script by parsing it as an async function body, not with `node --check`: `explorations/coordinator/tools/workflow-scenarios.js`.

## A second session

A second coordinating session contributes reviews and their commits, on a branch of its own from `main`. It runs no batch and does not change PLAN's order.

# Climb batch 13

## 1. For the curator

### The words this record uses

- **Walk** is the interpreter. It runs a program without static types. The **compiled path** checks a program's types with the **checker**, then makes JVM bytecode.
- **The one library** is the interpreter's library (`Library/`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`). At the **switch-over** the compiled path takes it over.
- **The distance** is the number of errors the checker reports on the one library. Each error has a **site** (a file and a line). This record counts sites by the ledger **row** that records their defect, not by the stage's classes (row 577). Phase 3 brings the distance to a true zero.
- **The count** is the older measure, the checker's errors on the one library's api files. It is 1: `isLeftZero` (row 582). This batch takes it to 0.

content.content:
## Preparing a batch record

An Opus planning worker drafts `CLIMB-BATCH-<n>.md`. A Fable reviewer edits it in place with one reason per change. The coordinator reads the diff and brings the record's questions to the curator one per message. The batch launches on the answers or on the standing go (P-121, "The phase-3 batches run on a standing go.").

The planner builds each rung's briefing as in-context learning: the agents were not trained on Fortress, and the language was never finished (P-109, "The mission briefing."). A briefing holds what the rung's section cites: the decisions and earlier rulings it rests on, its ledger rows, the specification's sections whole by their headings, the notes on the subject by section, and the library code that is the precedent. Process positions and harness facts stay out, because the brief's role text and the skill carry them. In batch 10 the workers named none of the 87 POSITIONS and FACTS keys before their fix edits (`process-engineering/context-study.md`, section 5). Each key goes through `facts-extract.sh --check` on the base, every key matching exactly one place. Each carries one line on why it is there. The planner marks the `checks` sub-list: the decisions and rows the checks need, and the sections and precedent code they compare against.

A rung that changes what an implementation does is briefed with the Appendix I Effects and the specification's notes that its change makes false, found by a grep while the record is prepared. Batch 9's record gave rung K none, and Appendix I's `comprises` Effect was that batch's one blocking finding (`reviews/batch-9-review.md`, finding 3).

A record asks a rung for no corpus-wide output comparison, no ladder before-run, no microGPT check and no specification build log (P-103, "The suite's verdict is the check."; "No re-measuring what the record holds."). Whole suites are the skill's rule (`tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite"). A count of the programs a change reaches, when a decision needs one, is the planner's probe, taken before the record is written. A named one-time count of changed outputs is asked only where a decision of the curator's names it for that rung. The coordinator starts its base pass before the launch (`tools/count-run/count-run.sh`).

The record's section on how it is run gives the manifest's fields rung by rung, the intro every agent reads, and the launch steps. It holds no copy of the block: the batch's generator writes the block from the record.

## Before the launch

The coordinator, in this order:

1. The script, this manual and the batch's manifest generator on `main`. The base is `main`'s head after them, by its full hash, passed as `args.base`.
2. The batch's one base build, a worktree at the base outside the main tree, built once and then left alone. Every rung worktree is seeded from it, and the old code runs from it (P-104, "Nothing is built or run twice on the same code."). About 200 s, as the skill's `worktrees.md`, "Finding or building a base build", gives it:

        git -C /home/user/fortress worktree add --detach /home/user/fortress-base<N> <base>
        cd /home/user/fortress-base<N>      # then set up the call as the skill's build-and-caches.md says
        ant compileAll                      # BUILD SUCCESSFUL
        # the library order (build-and-caches.md, "The library order"), then one walk run, which warms walk's caches:
        bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss
        git status --porcelain              # empty: the seed refuses a base build that is not clean

   Its path goes to the launch as `args.baseBuild`. The script refuses to start without it (scenario B1).
3. One trial seed proves the base build, about 3 s: `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh /home/user/fortress-base<N> /home/user/fortress-seedcheck - <base>`, then `git -C /home/user/fortress worktree remove /home/user/fortress-seedcheck`. One `old-fortress.sh /home/user/fortress-base<N> /home/user/fortress-seedcheck-caches ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss`, run from the main tree, proves the old code runs; its folder is removed after.
4. The briefings checked on the base (`python3 explorations/compile-ladder/plan-<N>/manifest/lists<N>.py`). The block generated (`gen<N>.py`), checked in a scratch copy and spliced (`check<N>.js`, then `check<N>.js --write`). Then `node explorations/coordinator/tools/workflow-scenarios.js` on the spliced script, which also checks that every skill section the script cites by name is a heading of the skill. Then the commit.
5. `df -h /` against one seeded worktree per rung (about 206 MB each) and the base build. `git status --porcelain` empty in the main tree, and no other agent writing there or pushing `main` while the run gathers and commits. The session's permission rules let the commit stage run `tools/mg-run.sh`.
6. Check-ins armed for the run's length, 45 minutes apart (P-127, "Check-ins and stops.").

The launch: `Workflow({scriptPath: 'explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js', args: {base: '<full hash>', baseBuild: '/home/user/fortress-base<N>'}})`. The args are kept byte for byte, since a resume needs them. The base build stays until the coordinator removes it after the landing.

Yes, two of your answers would let batch 14 do more. The record's queue names them:

- the self-typed bodies, batch 14's biggest candidate;
- whether a broader body can define an inherited abstract method (item 51).

The planner will list anything else it finds, each with a default. Here's the first.

**Should the checker treat `self` in a self-typed trait as the type that implements the trait?**

- A self-typed trait is a generic trait whose parameter stands for the type that implements it. An example is `trait Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]`.
- The checker types `self` there as `Integral[\I\]`, not as `I`. So it refuses 30 of the team's library bodies from 2008, each of which returns `self` or passes it on as an `I`. Walk runs all of them.
- They're 30 of the 85 errors left before the switch-over, the biggest group.
- Scala and Rust handle this with one rule: whatever implements the trait at `A` is an `A`, checked at each implementing type.
- The team's own idiom was a `comprises` clause that names the parameter. Their 2012 calculus dropped it.
- This is already measured. The checker rule, kept to method bodies, is a 114-line patch. It clears 29 errors, adds none, and doesn't slow the checker.
- A Fable check against the POPL 2019 paper found the rule sound, as long as the self type stays out of declared signatures.

Options:

1. **A checker rule, the Scala and Rust way.** The checker and the specification change, and the library and walk don't. It clears 29.
2. **The team's clause on seven traits.** The library, walk and the specification change. It once overflowed the checker. It clears 29.
3. **A cast in 21 library lines.** It clears 29, but the type is checked when the program runs instead of before.

Under any option, the 30th error is fixed by one body for each integer type.

A yes adds one checker rung to batch 14, and no walk result changes. It also changes the record's reading that no self type enters the library. A no leaves the 30 errors, and batch 14 runs without that rung.

I recommend 1.

# Planning the road

`explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md` holds the phases, the questions for the curator in the order they are needed, and the parked items. Keep every open question there, in the order it needs deciding, and none only in your context.

**nine steps**
: Order in which a fork is answered from the evidence before it reaches the curator: (1) what the mathematics says; (2) what each path does today, measured; (3) what the specification says under every spelling; (4) what the library does in the same family; (5) where the designers departed from Java; (6) what peer languages and their implementations do; (7) what the commits say; (8) the derivation from the curator's principles in POSITIONS; (9) the decision, in the curator's words.

**re-approval rows**
: Earlier decisions put to the curator again, parked in PLAN, "Off the path, parked".

## Procedures

- Ask for the curator's answers in PLAN's order. Raise the re-approval rows and other parked items only when the work reaches them.
- If a probe can settle a known fork, run it while you plan, before the batch is briefed. Put its result to the curator as an ask, so that the worker gets a task with the decision made.
- Answer a fork by the nine steps before you put it to the curator. Seek one global rule from type theory and the peers' implementations, not a rule on a rule.
- In the ask, name the library's own way first. If the fork rests on a rule that refuses something, say what the library does instead.
- Put rows to the curator one theme per message, each row in detail, with a refresher: other languages, and what makes sense in a high-performance language. The count of reversals is not the measure.
- Give idle time to the parked research in PLAN. It needs no go, but a new deliverable does: discuss it with the curator before you make it.
- Park what needs the curator's machine; do not simulate it.

content.content:
### Way 2: the team's `cast`

- Library only, 21 lines, clears 29; the team's own `cast[\T\]` (`:33-37`) and the team's own typecase on a trait's parameter inside its functional method (`Contains.MATCH`, `:1093-1098`). Nothing else changes.
- Against it. It is Java's answer: a static fact becomes a run-time check, at every call of every default body, and it tells the checker nothing, so every future body of the same shape pays it again. It is a per-site patch repeated 21 times, which is the "rule slapped on a rule" his position refuses, and it reads as the user-side workaround his library rule rules out. Its deciding unknown is walk's binding of a trait's parameter inside a functional method's body (ways note, way 2), and whether the code generator compiles a cast at a trait's parameter in a default body is unmeasured (row 426 covers a function's parameter only).
- Its place: the fallback if the recommended way's one measurement fails (section 6).

### Way 5: the team's idiom, `comprises T` on seven traits

- What it has. It is the team's own built device (Ryu, 2009, `3a8ad3b67`; Allen, 2011, `dbc91f830`), its meaning is already in the specification (`var-ref.tex:63-69`), the compiler library spells it, and Naden's 2012 text names it as the realisation of the idiom. The checker needs no change.
- What it costs. Three areas move. The library: one clause on each of seven traits in two files (the hierarchy rule forces `LexicographicOrder`, `MultiplicativeRing` and the orders to carry it together, `traits.tex:241-248`; route C's experiment found the same, "the clauses go on the whole family or on none of it", `route-c-experiment.md:104`). The ask form's yes/no line conflicts with the rule against do-nothing options. My "no" was one of those, and I should have weighed the options against each other. Holding.

No, it doesn't need the nine steps: they were run on 9 October. A worker went through the nine steps over every way, a Fable judgement weighed them, and a second Fable check tested the result against the POPL 2019 paper. What you're missing is the trade-offs in plain words, so here they are.

**1. The checker rule (Scala and Rust)**
- For: the team's library bodies stay exactly as written, walk doesn't change, and nothing is checked at run time.
- For: it's one general rule, and it's already measured: 29 errors cleared, none new, and no slowdown.
- Against: it's the revival's own rule, which no team text states. The team's own test of "self-typed" was the clause in option 2.
- Against: the specification gains two sentences and an entry in its appendix of changes.

**2. The team's clause, `comprises I`, on seven traits**
- For: it's the team's own device, built by Ryu in 2009 and Allen in 2011, and the specification has described it since 2009. Naden named it as the way to express this. The checker doesn't change.
- Against: three areas change. The library gets the clause on all seven traits at once, because the type hierarchy forces them together. Walk crashes with a stack overflow at load on any such clause today, so it needs a fix first. The specification must allow a type variable in a `comprises` clause, which the team's 2012 calculus removed. The revival also kept that door shut on purpose when it revised `comprises`.
- Against: the clause does more than type `self`. It closes each trait to its parameter, so exclusion and hierarchy checks can move for every instantiation, on both walk and the compiled path. On the old nested tower, eight such clauses overflowed the checker. On today's flat library it's unmeasured, so it needs a measurement run before a batch.

**3. The team's `cast`, in 21 library lines**

   - Welterweight (2012) types `self` in a trait as the plain trait type `T[P]` (`Papers/Welterweight/fig-wellformeddecls.tick:55`), admits only constructed types in a `comprises` clause (`fig-grammar.tick:6-8`, `:33-37`), and leaves its "Self-typed generics" dispatch step commented out with the placeholder "{\it Explanation of how this works}" (`dispatch.tick:195-210`).
   - Naden (2012-08-31, the latest dated text): "The self-type idiom is realized with the comprises clause ... the type Ring[X] is identified as X" (`justificationOfRTR.tex:580-582`); and, after showing that the idiom as a first-class type breaks the Return Type Rule on the nested tower, "the self-type idiom should be more than simply an idiom and instead a separate construct which cannot be used as a first class type, but instead only in bounds" (`:626-630`).
   - POPL 2019 has no self types and no tower (`research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md:280`, `:328-329`).
   - The later Types chapter says nothing of `self`; its `comprises` sentence lists "types and generic types determined by the generic type of the declaration" (`types.tick:384-389`), and Luchangco's comment beside it wants every listed type to be a trait type (`:245`).

A listed reference "is a declared trait identifier" (`traits.tex:163-165`), and the revival's `comprises` passage left a bare type variable in a clause open on purpose (`rung-spec-comprises/decision-record.md:19`, `:48`). - Whether a body returning `self` as `I` links and runs on the compiled path (the switch-over's).

First, a correction: no option removes `comprises`. Today the team's interpreter library has no self-typed clause at all. Option 2 would add one, `comprises I`, with a type variable in it, to seven traits. The team's compiler library does use that form.

**Does POPL 2019 help?**

Not with the choice. The paper has no self types, no number tower and no `comprises`; it drops closed types and says they "could be added back in an obvious way" without showing how. So it models neither option 1 nor option 2.

It does constrain how option 1 is built. The paper's proofs assume a declared signature never holds a type parameter inside an intersection. The first try at option 1 put `self`'s type, `Integral[\I\] & I`, into method signatures and got 18 false errors, exactly where the paper warns. The measured version keeps it inside method bodies only, and the Fable check found that this keeps it within the paper's ground.

**How clear is the later team signal?**

It's fairly clear against option 2 and only indirect for option 1:

- **Welterweight (2012)**, the team's last calculus, allows only named types in a `comprises` clause, never a type variable. Its self-typed dispatch step is commented out, with a placeholder: "Explanation of how this works".
- **The later Types chapter (2012)** lists only types made from the trait's own generic type. Luchangco's comment beside it wants every listed type to be a trait type.
- **Naden (31 August 2012)**, the latest dated text, says the idiom is realized with `comprises`. Then he shows that, used as an ordinary type, it breaks the Return Type Rule on the nested tower. He concludes it "should be ... a separate construct which cannot be used as a first class type, but instead only in bounds".
- No team text states option 1's rule. Option 1 comes closest to Naden's "only in bounds": it reads the self type from the bound the library already writes, and it never becomes a type you can write. That's my reading, not his words.

**Your earlier decisions that bear on it**

- Your decision that the type group's later word outweighs the early text. Read with the three texts above, it leans against adding the type-variable clause in option 2.
- Your `AnyIntegral` closure decision. There you had the checker read the library as the team meant it, rather than rewriting the library to suit the checker. Option 1 is the same move.
- "The library's own practice is the standard", with no workaround on the user's side. That leans against option 3's cast.
- The rule to seek one general rule from type theory and the peers, not a rule on top of a rule. That's for option 1 and against option 3's 21 patches.
- Route A, the exclusion rule kept and the number tower flat. Your words name only those two, but the record also reads route A as "no self type enters the library". That reading came from the batch 8 record and an earlier judge, not from you. Option 2 would write a self type into the library's text. Option 1 doesn't, though the checker gives `self` one.
- At batch 8's question you deferred this "until there is better information". That information is now on file.

So your own decisions point to option 1. The team's later texts argue against option 2 more clearly than they argue for option 1.
